transcript.heading: News Report One (American Male)
paras: Health officials in Canada announced new guidelines this week recommending that adults get at least 150 minutes of moderate physical activity per week, while also emphasizing the importance of reducing sedentary time for people of all ages. The updated guidelines, which replace recommendations from 10 years ago, now include specific advice that even small amounts of physical activity—just a few minutes at a time—can provide meaningful health benefits. Officials say that previous guidelines focused on longer exercise sessions led many people to believe they couldn't meet the requirements, but research now shows that short bursts of activity throughout the day, such as taking stairs, walking during breaks, or doing household chores, add up to significant health improvements. The guidelines also recommend muscle-strengthening activities at least twice per week for adults and older adults, along with balance exercises for seniors to prevent falls. Early data suggests that nearly 80 percent of Canadian adults currently do not meet the previous activity guidelines, a pattern that health officials hope to reverse with the more flexible recommendations.

transcript.heading: News Report Two (British Male)
paras: A rare copy of the first printed collection of William Shakespeare's plays, known as the First Folio, has sold at auction in New York for a record-breaking 9.98 million dollars, making it the most expensive work of literature ever sold at auction. The 1623 First Folio, published seven years after Shakespeare's death, contains 36 of his plays, 18 of which—including *Macbeth*, *The Tempest*, and *Julius Caesar*—would have been lost forever if they had not been included in this collection, as no earlier printed versions exist. Only about 235 copies of the First Folio are known to survive today, most held in museums and library collections, making copies that come up for sale extremely rare and highly sought after by collectors and institutions. The copy sold this week was one of only a few complete copies remaining in private hands and was described by auction officials as being in unusually good condition for its nearly 400-year age. The buyer, who chose to remain anonymous, purchased the book through a telephone bid after more than five minutes of competitive bidding.

transcript.heading: News Report Three (American Female)
paras: South Korea announced this week that it will begin offering free menstrual hygiene products in all public schools and public restrooms in government buildings starting next year, becoming one of the first countries in the world to implement such a universal program. The initiative was approved by the National Assembly following years of advocacy by women's rights groups, who argued that access to menstrual products is a basic health necessity and that cost barriers prevent many low-income girls and women from attending school or work regularly. Government officials estimate the program will cost approximately 25 million dollars annually and will benefit an estimated 12 million people. In addition to free products, the program includes funding for menstrual health education in schools and efforts to reduce the stigma surrounding menstruation. Several other countries, including Scotland and New Zealand, have implemented similar programs in schools, but South Korea's program is among the most comprehensive, extending to all public facilities. Officials say they will also work with private businesses to encourage them to provide free products in workplace restrooms as well.

transcript.heading: Conversation One (British Male + American Female)
paras: Man (Mike): Hey Chloe, how's your new apartment working out? You moved in a couple weeks ago, right? How does it compare to your old place?

Woman (Chloe): Oh, I love it for the most part! The location is perfect—it's only a 10-minute walk to campus and there are lots of great restaurants and coffee shops nearby. The building itself is really nice too; it has a gym and a rooftop terrace. But honestly, I'm having a little bit of trouble with my new roommate.
Man: Oh no, that's a shame. What's going on? Is she messy or loud or something? You guys got along pretty well when you met before moving in, right?

Woman: We did! She's really friendly, and she's super clean actually—that's not the problem at all. It's just that our sleep schedules are completely different and we have very different ideas about having people over. She works evenings at a restaurant, so she gets home around 11:30 or midnight most nights, and then she likes to watch TV and cook when she gets home, which is when I'm usually trying to sleep because I have early morning classes three days a week. And she has her boyfriend over almost every night, which I didn't expect. I don't mind him—he's nice—but I feel like I don't have as much privacy as I thought I would.
Man: That sounds really frustrating. Have you talked to her about it yet? Sometimes roommates don't even realize they're bothering you unless you say something directly.

Woman: I've been putting it off because I don't want to start off on the wrong foot and make things awkward. But you're right, I probably should say something soon before it starts really bothering me. I was thinking maybe we could set up some kind of roommate agreement—like, no loud noise after 11 on weeknights, and maybe let each other know when we're having people stay over?

Man: That sounds like a really good approach. You could frame it positively, like "I really like living here, and I think if we both have clear expectations, it'll work out great for everyone." Most reasonable people are open to that kind of conversation. If you want, I could help you think through what points to bring up.

Woman: That would be awesome, actually. I want to make sure I'm being fair too—she also has a right to feel at home here. I don't want to sound like I'm complaining the whole time. We're both paying rent, after all.

Man: Exactly. Compromise is key. Maybe she can use headphones when she watches TV at night, and you guys can agree on how many nights a week having guests over is reasonable. You'll probably find that she's totally open to figuring something out.
Woman: You're right. I'll talk to her this weekend when we both have some free time. Thanks for listening and giving me advice, Mike—it helps to talk it through.

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (American Male + British Female)

I went to her review session before the first quiz, and it was really helpful—she basically went over all the key concepts that ended up being tested and gave us a good idea of what format the questions would be. That helped me a lot when I was studying for the quiz. I can send it to you later today if you want. For genetics, I would recommend working through the practice problems at the end of each chapter in the textbook—Professor Chen uses really similar problems on her exams, just with different numbers and scenarios.

I find if I study for an hour or two every day, I remember things much better than if I try to study for eight hours the night before. Would you want to study together tonight in the library? transcript.heading: Passage One (British Female)
paras: The Great Barrier Reef, located off the northeastern coast of Australia, is the world's largest coral reef system and one of the most biodiverse ecosystems on Earth. Stretching over 2,300 kilometers and covering an area of approximately 344,400 square kilometers, the reef is so large that it can be seen from outer space and is often considered one of the natural wonders of the world. The reef is composed of over 2,900 individual reefs and 900 islands, built by billions of tiny organisms called coral polyps, which secrete calcium carbonate to form hard skeletons that build up over thousands of years. The Great Barrier Reef is home to an extraordinary variety of marine life, including more than 1,500 species of fish, 400 types of coral, 30 species of whales and dolphins, 6 species of sea turtles, and around 200 species of birds, making it a critical habitat for many endangered and vulnerable species. It also supports a tourism industry worth billions of dollars annually, attracting millions of visitors who come to snorkel, dive, and experience the reef's natural beauty. Unfortunately, the reef faces severe threats from climate change, which causes rising ocean temperatures that lead to coral bleaching—a process where corals expel the symbiotic algae that give them color and nutrients, often resulting in death if temperatures remain high. Other threats include pollution from agricultural runoff, coastal development, overfishing, and outbreaks of crown-of-thorns starfish that feed on coral. Scientists estimate that the reef has lost more than half of its coral cover since 1985, prompting widespread conservation efforts to protect and restore this unique ecosystem.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (American Male)
paras: Public libraries in the United States have undergone dramatic transformations over the past 25 years, evolving from quiet buildings primarily focused on lending books into dynamic community centers offering a wide range of free services and resources for people of all ages and backgrounds. While books and reading remain central to their mission, modern libraries now offer far more than just printed materials. Most public libraries provide free access to computers and high-speed internet, a critical service for people without internet access at home who need to apply for jobs, do schoolwork, access government services, or communicate with family. Many libraries offer free classes in computer skills, resume writing, English as a second language, financial literacy, and even basic coding and robotics for children and adults. Most systems also offer digital media lending, including e-books, audiobooks, movies, and music that patrons can download to their devices without visiting the building in person. During economic recessions, libraries often see significant increases in usage as people rely on them for resources to find jobs and access free entertainment and education. During the COVID-19 pandemic, many libraries adapted quickly, offering curbside pickup of books, virtual programs and storytimes, and expanded Wi-Fi access in parking lots for people who needed internet at home. Librarians themselves have seen their roles expand beyond helping people find books; many now serve as information specialists, technology tutors, social service navigators, and community organizers, helping connect people with resources ranging from housing assistance to mental health services. Despite their growing importance, many public library systems face challenges from budget cuts and debates about the appropriate role of libraries in the digital age. However, public support for libraries remains strong, with surveys consistently showing that libraries are among the most trusted and valued public institutions in American communities.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (British Male)
paras: The development of written language is one of the most important achievements in human history, allowing people to record information, communicate across distances, and pass knowledge down from generation to generation in ways that oral tradition alone could not achieve. The earliest known writing systems emerged independently in several different regions of the world beginning around 5,500 years ago. The first true writing system is generally believed to be cuneiform, developed by the Sumerian civilization in Mesopotamia (present-day Iraq) around 3500 BCE, which used wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay tablets with a reed stylus. Initially, cuneiform was used for simple record-keeping—tracking trade transactions, tax records, and agricultural yields—but over time it evolved to represent spoken language more completely, allowing people to write literature, laws, religious texts, and personal letters. In Egypt, hieroglyphic writing developed around 3200 BCE, using a combination of pictorial symbols that could represent sounds, words, or concepts. Writing systems also developed independently in other parts of the world, including Chinese characters around 1200 BCE and Maya script in Mesoamerica around 300 BCE. The invention of the alphabet, where symbols represent individual sounds rather than whole words or concepts, was a major innovation that made writing more accessible and easier to learn. The first consonantal alphabet emerged around 1800 BCE in the eastern Mediterranean, and the Greek alphabet, developed around 800 BCE, was the first to include symbols for vowels as well, forming the basis of many modern alphabets including the Latin alphabet used for English. Before the invention of the printing press in the 15th century, all texts had to be copied by hand, making books extremely rare and expensive, and literacy was limited to a small elite. The printing press revolutionized access to written materials, allowing books to be produced quickly and cheaply, leading to widespread increases in literacy and transforming education, science, religion, and politics.
